documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the AllyAI Agent Product Hub – a comprehensive internal enablement guide and resource center for all AllyAI agent products. An enablement guide is a centralized internal document that aggregates training materials, pitch assets, demo scripts, competitive positioning, pricing tools, certification requirements, and product contacts to support sales teams in successfully positioning and selling the product. This hub is used by Account Executives, Sales Engineers, and GTM teams to prepare for first calls, second calls, demos, certifications, and competitive deals.

The document covers all AllyAI agents: Sales Agent, Shelf Agent, Content Agent, and Media Agent. It includes links to internal trainings (SKO 2026 recordings with passwords, Day 1 & Day 2 video links, audio transcripts), first call and second call pitch decks (including the “Agentic” deck), demo scripts, datasheets, landing pages, and messaging documents. It outlines certification requirements (70% passing grade, manager + PMM reviewers, Zoom recording submissions, April 1 deadline, resubmission policy), and provides instructions for dry runs 48 hours before first opportunities. It also references pricing resources such as country-based pricing and a Sales Agent pricing calculator.

A major section focuses on Sales Agent positioning as "Your 24x7 Junior Analyst for Growth" and "Copilot for Amazon," highlighting conversational AI capabilities (Ask AllyAI), root cause analysis, gap-to-plan recommendations, unified data, and end-to-end automation across operational and financial workflows. It details capabilities like dispute management, chargeback recovery, shortage tracking, deduction recovery ($200+ million recovered), 3+ billion automations, 2,500+ annual FTE hours saved, and integration with Amazon ticketing systems. It emphasizes unified insights across Sales, Operations, Content, Advertising, Market Share, AMC insights, incrementality reporting, and category-level dashboards across 100s of categories.

The hub also contains competitive positioning and FUD talk tracks against Stackline, Shalion, and DSA providers, including prompts around weekly data updates, black-box transparency, unproven automations, and limited integrations. It includes Digital Shelf Analytics positioning (Digital Shelf 360), CIQ strengths such as intraday scraping, custom reporting, store-level availability data, and seamless retail media integration. It contrasts legacy SEO-based tools with Content Agent optimization for AI-driven experiences like Amazon Rufus and GEO. There are structured sales prompts, objection-handling questions, digital shelf comparison frameworks, and cross-functional value messaging for Category Management, Brand, Shopper Marketing, Sales, Supply Chain, and Finance teams.

Use this document if someone asks for: "Where are all AllyAI agent resources?", "Sales Agent certification requirements", "Sales Agent demo script", "Stackline competitive positioning", "Digital Shelf 360 comparison", "SKO training recordings", or "Sales Agent pricing calculator." It is the master navigation hub for AllyAI-related GTM materials.

Do not confuse this with a specific Sales Agent First Call Deck or Second Call Deck, which are standalone customer-facing presentations. It is also not a Product Box (which defines positioning and value proposition at a strategic level) or a Battle Card (which focuses narrowly on competitor comparisons). Instead, this hub aggregates and links to all of those materials.

documents.documentIdentity: This is the Sales Agent Certification - an internal enablement and evaluation guide outlining the requirements, pitch structure, demo flow, scoring criteria, resources, and submission process for certifying sales reps on the AllyAI Sales Agent product. It details exactly how reps must deliver the Sales Agent Pitch and Demo, what materials to use (2nd Call Deck, Demo Script, Demo Link), certification logistics (70% passing grade, Zoom recordings, Google Form submission), deadlines (March 17 training, April 1 submission, April 10 feedback), and required dry runs prior to live opportunities.
documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Sales Agent Certification - an internal sales enablement and certification guide that defines how sales representatives are evaluated and approved to sell and demo AllyAI Sales Agent. An enablement guide like this establishes training expectations, certification criteria, required materials, scoring thresholds, timelines, and coaching processes. It is used internally by sales reps, managers, and PMM to ensure consistent messaging and demo quality before reps take Sales Agent into live customer conversations.

The document is structured around two core certification components: the Sales Agent Pitch and the Sales Agent Demo. For the Pitch, reps must use the "2nd Call Deck_Sales Agent" and walk through current business challenges, articulate the data overload problem, explain what AllyAI Sales Agent is and its value, present a customer story and holistic impact, and clearly communicate the main idea of each slide. For the Demo, reps must follow the "Demo_Sales Agent" script and demo link, start with a strong hook (reiterating the reporting and data overload challenge), showcase the Command Center gap-to-plan view across categories and retailers, demonstrate RCA (root cause analysis) at the SKU level with recommendations, and use Ask Ally in a conversational Q&A format with a follow-up question. The demo must conclude by reinforcing outcomes: instant visibility, actionable recommendations, and hours saved.

The certification logistics are clearly defined: a passing grade of 70%, reviewers include the rep’s manager plus PMM, and submissions require Zoom recordings of both the Sales Agent pitch and demo. Recordings must be submitted via Google Form (with passwords) by Wednesday, April 1, with feedback delivered by Friday, April 10. Any score below 70% requires coaching and mandatory resubmission. The document also references key enablement resources including the First Call Pitch Deck - Agentic, SKO Recording (S88F&n&L), Sales Agent 2nd Call / Pitch Deck, Demo Script, Datasheet Draft, Landing Page, Messaging Document, Product Box - Copilot for Amazon, Product Box - Sales Agent, and the GTM Enablement > AllyAI > Sales Agent hub.

Additionally, the guide mandates a Dry Run Pitch at least 48 hours prior to a rep’s first Sales Agent opportunity. This dry run must be scheduled with the sales manager and a PMM to provide coaching, tailor the pitch to specific scenarios, and tighten the feedback loop to increase win rates. The document also references Sales Agent Pricing with Calculator and Country-Based Pricing (excluding market share), signaling alignment between certification and commercial readiness.

Use this document when someone asks: “What are the requirements to get Sales Agent certified?”, “What’s the passing score for Sales Agent demo certification?”, “How do I submit my Sales Agent pitch recording?”, “What’s included in the Sales Agent certification process?”, or “What do I need to cover in the Sales Agent demo?”

Not to confuse with: the Sales Agent 2nd Call / Pitch Deck (customer-facing presentation content), the Demo Script (step-by-step talk track for live demo delivery), the Product Box - Sales Agent (product definition and positioning), or the Sales Agent Datasheet (external summary of features and benefits). This document is about internal certification and evaluation—not customer-facing messaging alone.

Effective date references include Certification Training on March 17, submission deadline Wednesday, April 1, and feedback by Friday, April 10. Messaging is noted as still being refined, indicating this is an active and evolving enablement document.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Digital Shelf Optimization - Competitive Intelligence deck - a competitive battlecard-style sales enablement document designed to help sellers position CommerceIQ’s Digital Shelf Analytics (DSA) against key competitors including Stackline, Shalion, Data Impact, and Omni & Beacon. A battlecard is a competitive sales tool used in live deals to differentiate against specific vendors, handle objections, introduce FUD (fear, uncertainty, doubt) questions, and reinforce product strengths with clear capability comparisons. This document is intended for active opportunities where a prospect is evaluating alternative digital shelf analytics providers.

The document includes structured competitive sections by vendor, each outlining CommerceIQ strengths and competitive gaps. Core CIQ differentiators highlighted include intraday scraping (up to 6 times per day, and up to 24 times per day for top SKUs and keywords), real-time data integration, seamless integration with Retail Media including 24/7 bid optimization driven by share of voice and availability metrics, comprehensive retailer coverage (900+ retailers across 50+ countries), store-level availability data, custom reporting and dashboards, and data transparency versus "black box" approaches. The deck repeatedly contrasts CIQ’s near real-time updates with competitors offering weekly scraping (e.g., Stackline), positioning this as a critical disadvantage in fast-moving eCommerce environments.

The content also includes embedded FUD discovery questions such as: concerns about weekly data updates, reliance on unproven automations (Stackline), limited integrations with retail media, black-box data transparency issues, and responsiveness to evolving eCommerce trends. There are comparison frameworks such as "Digital Shelf Comparison for DSA" and product-specific breakdowns (e.g., Digital Shelf 360, Data Impact Digital Shelf, Omni & Beacon). The Shalion section highlights claimed differentiators such as geolocation data and regional marketplace insights, while clarifying that some competitive intelligence capabilities are not unique. CIQ’s broader platform strengths are reinforced, including AI-driven automation, profit recovery automation, predictive analytics for demand forecasting, market share analytics, sales and POS integration, and detailed onboarding and continuous support.

Additionally, the document emphasizes CommerceIQ’s unified all-in-one platform approach, connecting Digital Shelf Analytics with Sales, POS, Advertising, and Availability data for a single performance view. It highlights mobile app coverage, global scalability, automated retail media bidding, and real-time analytics across systems. Repeated positioning themes include agility, innovation, independence, and proactive adaptation to new eCommerce trends.

Use this document when a prospect says they are evaluating Stackline, Shalion, Data Impact, or Omni & Beacon; when objections arise around data frequency, integrations, or retail media alignment; or when a rep needs targeted competitive questions to introduce doubt about weekly scraping, limited integrations, or unproven automations. It is particularly useful in mid-to-late stage deals where competitive displacement or differentiation is required.

Not to confuse with a Digital Shelf product datasheet (which would describe features without competitive framing), a Second Call Deck (which would provide broader solution walkthrough and pricing), or a Retail Media Management battlecard (which focuses specifically on advertising competitors like Pacvue or Skai). This document is specifically focused on Digital Shelf Analytics competitive positioning.

This is the AllyAI Sales Agent 2nd Call Deck – a detailed follow-up sales presentation designed for second meetings with prospective Amazon brands and CPG companies. A second call deck is used after an initial discovery conversation to go deeper into product capabilities, business impact, use cases, automation workflows, AI functionality, proof points, and quantified results. This deck positions AllyAI Sales Agent as an “AI Junior Analyst for Growth” that helps commercial teams accelerate decisions and hit their sales plan on Amazon.

The deck opens by framing core business challenges on Amazon: contracting margins, tariffs and rising media spend increasing COGS, AI-driven shifts in consumer behavior (e.g., Rufus changing the path to purchase), and data overload for CPG ecommerce leaders. It highlights common commercial questions (e.g., "Which SKUs are driving the most revenue right now?", "How has conversion rate trended over the last 90 days?", "What actions should I take to recover declining sales?", "How should I adjust pricing without sacrificing margin?", "Which products should I replenish to avoid stockouts?") and introduces AllyAI as a 24x7 conversational AI trained on 100k+ hours of commerce scenarios that delivers root cause analysis and recommendations instantly.

Core capabilities include Unified Sales Intelligence (one platform combining sales, operations, content, advertising, and market share insights), Gap-to-Plan forecasting with AI recommendations, conversational sales diagnostics, automated QBR generation, dashboards by category and SKU, AMC Insights and incrementality reporting, retail media reporting, and Amazon Command Center visibility. The deck emphasizes AI automations across operational and financial workflows, including dispute management (chargebacks, shortages, deductions), direct integration with Amazon ticketing systems, automated reporting and alerts, and multi-phase dispute processes that can recover up to 8x lost revenue and profit. It also highlights reduction of reporting time by 50% through AI-generated reports and prevention of sales leakage via inventory forecasting and in-stock optimization.

Proof points and scale metrics are featured prominently: 3+ billion automations executed, 6 of the top 10 CPG brands as CommerceIQ customers, $200+ million in deductions recovered, and 2,500+ annual FTE hours saved with Sales Agent and the broader platform. A detailed case study outlines how a global pet food brand in a highly competitive category achieved $3.4M in Sales Management and Retail Media automations with 26% CAGR growth, improving ad efficiency, optimizing search and display ads, refining keyword targeting, streamlining digital shelf execution, and reducing manual workload to prevent revenue loss.

Use this deck when a prospect asks for a deeper dive into AllyAI Sales Agent capabilities, wants to understand gap-to-plan forecasting and root cause analysis, requests proof of ROI from automation and dispute recovery, or needs to see how CommerceIQ unifies sales, retail media, and digital shelf in one platform. documents.documentIdentity: This is the Content Agent Objections document – a centralized internal enablement guide capturing common customer objections about CommerceIQ’s Content Agent product, along with approved responses and positioning guidance to help sales, solutions, and product marketing teams address concerns during prospect and customer conversations.
documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Content Agent Objections document – an internal enablement guide that compiles recurring customer objections raised in sales meetings and calls about CommerceIQ’s Content Agent, along with structured responses from product marketing, solutions, and product teams. An enablement guide like this is designed to prepare customer-facing teams to confidently handle resistance, clarify misconceptions, and reinforce product differentiation during live conversations. It is not a pitch deck, but rather a tactical objection-handling resource.

The document includes detailed responses to concerns about PIM (Product Information Management) access, data quality, workflow constraints, and prior negative experiences with similar tools. For example, it addresses objections such as discomfort granting CommerceIQ access to PIM data by clarifying that Content Agent does not require full control and can operate with limited, read-only access or leverage PDP (Product Detail Page) and available product data. It reinforces that brands retain full control over approvals and publication. It also explains that Content Agent is designed to integrate into existing internal approval workflows, surfacing prioritized recommendations and draft content that teams can review before implementation.

A significant section addresses concerns about messy or unreliable PIM data. The document clarifies that unlike traditional PIM or syndication systems that simply push PIM content to retailer PDPs, Content Agent evaluates both PIM data and live PDP content to identify gaps, inconsistencies, and incorrect information. It can recommend updates to both the PIM and the retailer PDP, positioning the product as a system that improves overall PIM health over time rather than being dependent on pristine inputs.

The document also tackles skepticism from brands that have used legacy content optimization tools. It differentiates Content Agent from static SEO or completeness-based tools by emphasizing optimization for AI-driven retail experiences such as Amazon Rufus and GEO (Generative Engine Optimization). It reframes the idea of "already highly optimized" content by highlighting new opportunities for visibility, relevance, and conversion in AI-powered shopping environments.

Use this document when a prospect says: “We don’t want to give PIM access,” “Our internal approval process is too complex,” “Our PIM data is messy,” or “We’ve tried tools like this before and our content is already optimized.” It is particularly valuable in late-stage evaluations, security reviews, or technical validation calls where objections around data access, governance, and differentiation surface.

Not to confuse with: the Content Agent Product Box (which defines positioning, features, and pricing), the Content Agent First Call Deck (high-level value proposition and overview), or competitive battle cards (which focus specifically on head-to-head comparisons). This document is focused strictly on objection handling and internal alignment on messaging.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Demo_Sales Agent Script – a structured demo talk track designed to guide sales representatives through a compelling, narrative-driven demonstration of the AllyAI Sales Agent. A talk track is a scripted or semi-scripted sales enablement document that provides specific wording, transitions, and positioning guidance for live customer conversations. This document is intended for use during product demos, particularly early-stage or mid-funnel calls where the goal is to clearly articulate value and show the product in action.

The script begins with a strong hook designed to anchor the conversation in a common executive pain point: the time spent manually pulling reports to answer simple leadership questions such as “Why did sales drop last week?” It outlines typical diagnostic questions (pricing, traffic, media, SKU-level vs. category-level impact) and highlights the operational friction of exporting data, building pivots, and stitching together traffic, media, and inventory sources. The framing emphasizes delayed insights (“by the time you get the answer, the week's already over”) and positions Sales Agent as a faster, more direct alternative to traditional dashboard-based analysis.

The document explicitly contrasts Sales Agent with “other solutions” that require hours or days navigating dashboards and reports. It introduces Sales Agent as an AI-powered assistant that provides immediate answers, surfaces pacing vs. plan, identifies gaps, generates recommendations, and enables root cause analysis through natural-language questioning. The script uses the analogy of a “junior analyst who does all the heavy lifting for you, 24/7,” reinforcing automation, speed, and accessibility of insights.

The script also references a Demo Link (Generic Demo Link & Nestlé), implying a structured demo flow potentially anchored in a recognizable brand scenario. It includes a transition statement (“Let me show you how it works.”) to move from problem framing into live product demonstration. The focus is on showing how users can ask questions directly and receive synthesized, actionable answers without manually digging through reports.

Use this document if someone asks for: “Sales Agent demo script,” “How do I position Sales Agent in a live demo?”, “What’s the hook for Sales Agent?”, “How do I explain Sales Agent vs dashboards?”, or “What’s the talk track for a Nestlé demo?” It is particularly useful for new reps preparing for their first live demo or for standardizing messaging across the sales team.

Not to confuse with: a Sales Agent Product Box (which defines positioning, pricing, features, and competitive differentiation in detail), a First Call Deck (high-level overview for discovery), or a Second Call Deck (deep dive into features, implementation, and ROI). This document is specifically a spoken demo narrative, not a slide deck or pricing document.

This is the CIQ PMF Signal Report for March 3–9, 2026 — a weekly sales enablement and product-market fit diagnostic document. A PMF Signal Report is an internal GTM intelligence report that synthesizes live customer call data (via Gong) to evaluate how well product positioning aligns with buyer pain, where messaging is landing or failing, which objections are recurring, and which features or roadmap gaps are blocking revenue. It is used by Product Marketing (PMM), Sales Leadership, and Product teams to prioritize messaging changes, content creation, and roadmap decisions.

The report is structured into multiple analytical sections: (1) Message-Market Fit (what value propositions are landing vs. not landing), (2) Problem-Language Alignment (customer phrasing vs. CIQ positioning language), (3) Objection Patterns by segment (Enterprise, Mid-Market, EMEA win-back), (4) Aha Moment Detection (demo workflows that create strong buyer engagement), (5) Deal Velocity by Pain Category (average close time, win rate, PMF verdict), (6) PMF Signal Scorecard (quantified weekly PMF health across six dimensions), and (7) PMM Action Plan (this week vs. this month priorities). It explicitly names accounts such as Estee Lauder, Mars Wrigley, Kimberly Clark, Wahl Clipper, P&G, Danone, Newell, Coke, Tropicana EU, and Target Corporation.

documents.documentIdentity: This is the CIQ Service Level Agreement (SLA) - a formal contractual document defining CommerceIQ’s service availability commitment (99.5% monthly uptime), scheduled maintenance windows, service credit structure (5%, 7.5%, 10% tiers), SLA claim process, termination rights tied to sub-95% performance, and exclusive remedy terms. It outlines the specific conditions, exclusions, and financial remedies that apply if CommerceIQ fails to meet its uptime obligations.
documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the CIQ Service Level Agreement (SLA) - a legally binding service commitment document that defines CommerceIQ’s uptime guarantees, remedies, and customer rights in the event of service disruptions. An SLA is a contractual addendum that specifies measurable service performance standards (such as uptime percentages), outlines how performance is calculated, and details the financial or contractual remedies if those standards are not met. This document is used during procurement, legal review, and enterprise negotiations to clarify reliability commitments and risk mitigation.

The agreement establishes a 99.5% Service Availability commitment, measured over a calendar month and excluding Scheduled Downtime and defined exclusions. Scheduled Downtime is limited to a Maintenance Window from 2:00 am to 6:00 am Eastern Standard Time (EST). If downtime occurs outside this window, CommerceIQ must provide 24-hour advance notice. The document also clarifies that emergency downtime will be scheduled during the Maintenance Window when reasonably possible. Service Availability exclusions include events outside CIQ’s reasonable control, customer infrastructure or ISP issues, misuse outside the agreement scope, and customer acts or omissions.

The SLA defines a formal SLA Claims Process requiring customers to submit a support ticket within five (5) business days of the incident. CommerceIQ will investigate and make a good-faith determination of validity. If monthly availability drops below 99.5%, validated claims trigger Service Credits applied to the next invoice (not redeemable for cash). The credit tiers are clearly defined: 5.0% of the equivalent monthly fee for availability greater than 97.5% and less than or equal to 99.5%; 7.5% for greater than 95.0% and less than or equal to 97.5%; and 10.0% for less than or equal to 95.0%. Credits are capped at 10% of the affected CIQ Service’s monthly fee in any calendar month.

The agreement also defines an "SLA Termination Event," triggered if availability falls below 95% in any four (4) months during two (2) consecutive calendar quarters. In that scenario, either party may terminate for cause without opportunity to cure. For customers, termination replaces the service credit remedy for the affected month. The document explicitly states that the remedies described (service credits or termination) are the exclusive remedy for SLA failures and do not constitute a breach of the broader agreement.

Use this document when responding to questions such as: "What uptime does CIQ guarantee?", "What happens if CIQ goes down?", "How are service credits calculated?", "What is the SLA termination threshold?", or "What is the claims submission process?" It is especially relevant during security reviews, procurement negotiations, MSA redlines, and enterprise IT diligence.

Not to be confused with a Master Services Agreement (MSA), which governs broader contractual terms; a Security Overview, which addresses data protection controls; or a Product Datasheet, which describes features and functionality rather than contractual uptime guarantees. This document strictly governs availability commitments and remedies.

Last Updated: October 6, 2020. Status: Active unless superseded by a newer SLA version.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the CommerceIQ AI Retail Survey Report 2026 - a comprehensive research report and sales enablement asset that summarizes original survey data on AI adoption in retail and ecommerce. As an enablement guide, it is designed to arm sales, marketing, and leadership teams with data-backed insights to shape executive conversations, validate market demand, and position CommerceIQ’s AI agents as the future operating model for commerce teams. Use this document in strategic selling situations where credibility, industry benchmarks, and quantified market trends are required.

The report is based on a January 2026 study commissioned by CommerceIQ and conducted by Qualtrics, surveying 240 marketing and sales decision-makers at brands with $300M+ in annual ecommerce revenue across CPG, consumer electronics, grocery, health & household, and other categories selling through Amazon, Walmart, Target, and Instacart. It establishes that AI adoption is no longer exploratory: 71% of respondents are already very familiar with or actively using AI agents, 69% say their organization is ready to pilot or already using AI agents, 80% are likely or very likely to shift budget from agencies to AI-powered solutions (if performance matches), 82% expect AI investment to increase, and 86% are past the exploration phase.

The report details the top operational challenges AI is expected to solve: 46% say data isn’t actionable, 43% cite lack of data accessibility, 42% lack time to make decisions, 40% struggle with too much data, 32% report siloed data, and 31% say the pace of change is too fast to scale. It also outlines the "Non-Negotiable Requirements for AI Adoption," including data trust and quality (56%), stronger data security (53%), integration with existing systems (49%), decision transparency (49%), proven ROI (48%), unified business context (82% say very important or critical), and human-in-the-loop oversight (43%). The report emphasizes that commerce leaders reject black-box AI and siloed tools, demanding explainability, measurable outcomes, and unified visibility across sales, media, inventory, and digital shelf.

Additionally, the report identifies where leaders will invest first in 2026: retail media optimization, PDP/content optimization, predictive demand (17%), PIM compliance (13%), and AI agents that autonomously optimize media campaigns (26% cited as most exciting emerging capability). It contrasts AI agents with traditional agency models, noting that 55% believe agency costs don’t match results and that scaling from 500 SKUs across two retailers to 5,000 SKUs across ten retailers has created a structural capacity gap that manual models cannot close.

If someone asks: “Are commerce leaders actually ready for AI agents?”, “What percentage of brands will shift budget from agencies to AI?”, “What are the barriers to AI adoption in retail?”, “What proof points do we have about unified context and human oversight?”, or “Where are brands investing in AI in 2026?”, use this document. It is particularly effective in C-level and VP-level conversations where market validation and third-party research (Qualtrics) add authority.

Not to be confused with a product datasheet (which details specific CommerceIQ features), a pricing deck (which outlines commercial terms), or a competitive battle card (which compares vendors). This report is market-facing thought leadership and industry validation, not a feature-by-feature product breakdown.

A training deck is an internal enablement document used to align teams on product capabilities, value proposition, proof points, and positioning. This deck equips teams to confidently explain how the optimizer drives incremental growth, budget efficiency, and real-time bid automation using proprietary AI models.

The deck begins with the core value proposition: “Unlocking incremental growth and efficiency with AllyAI teammate.” It highlights quantified performance across 10 brands in Q1 2025, including +55% ad sales growth, +75% campaign performance improvement, -12.8% CPC reduction, +41.83% iROAS surge, +58.62% ad sales amplification, -16.21% CPC efficiency improvement, +51.2% traffic (clicks) growth, and +39.98% ROAS uplift. It emphasizes incrementality (iROAS) as the “true north” metric, positioning CommerceIQ’s real-time incrementality model against backward-looking MMM models with two-week delays and limited keyword/retailer support.

Core product capabilities are detailed extensively. The optimizer uses 50+ signals including incrementality (iROAS), digital shelf signals (price, promotion, availability, out-of-stock, competitor pricing), Amazon Marketing Stream hourly data, Walmart hourly CTR/clicks/impressions, and Share of Voice trends. It performs thousands of optimizations per day across thousands of keywords. Proprietary components include: ASAS (Campaign Potential Assessment System) to determine maximum efficient spend per campaign; 3D Bid Efficiency Frontiers to identify diminishing returns and optimal bids; and a Real-Time Optimization Flywheel that recalibrates budgets daily and weekly based on demand signals. The system dynamically reallocates daily budgets within constraints and predicts optimal bids using brand-specific models.

The deck also walks through product experience and controls: a simplified and guided UI for streamlined campaign setup; centralized bidding and budgeting to avoid rule conflicts; granular product- and target-level optimization; custom KPI alignment (iROAS, Share of Voice, total sales, ROAS); a live goal tracker dashboard; and integration of brand constraints including tentpole events (e.g., allocating 50% of monthly budget to BFCM). A featured customer quote from Aaron Conkey, Sr. Digital Manager at Pilgrim’s Pride, validates improvements in iROAS and sales while lowering CPC in a competitive poultry category.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the CIQ Mutual NDA - Sales/BD use.pdf - a Standard Reciprocal Mutual Non-Disclosure Agreement template used by CommerceIQ’s Sales and Business Development teams to formalize confidentiality obligations with prospects, customers, and partners. A Mutual NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) is a legally binding contract that allows two parties to exchange sensitive business, technical, financial, or customer information while protecting both sides from unauthorized disclosure or misuse. This document is intended for pre-contract discussions, evaluations, and early-stage commercial conversations.

The agreement defines key terms including “Confidential Information,” “Disclosing Party,” “Receiving Party,” and “Affiliate.” Confidential Information is broadly defined to include nonpublic information designated as confidential, information that should reasonably be treated as confidential under the circumstances, and information that by its nature would be treated as confidential. Explicit examples include technology and product information, business policies, trade secrets, financial data, customer data, and third-party information that the disclosing party is obligated to protect. The agreement also clearly outlines exclusions from Confidential Information, such as information that becomes publicly available without breach, was known prior to disclosure, is independently developed, or is received from a third party without breach of obligation.

The document specifies core obligations of the Receiving Party: (1) not to disclose Confidential Information except for the Permitted Purpose (evaluation of and engagement in the business opportunity between the parties), (2) to use at least reasonable care—no less than the care used to protect its own confidential information, (3) to limit disclosure to employees, directors, affiliates, advisors, agents, contractors, consultants, and interns on a need-to-know basis with appropriate legal duties of confidentiality, (4) to notify the Disclosing Party immediately upon discovery of unauthorized use or disclosure, and (5) upon request or termination, to return or certify destruction of Confidential Information (with limited retention in backups subject to continued confidentiality). The Confidentiality Period is explicitly set at 3 years from the date of first disclosure.

Additional legal provisions include: Governing Law (California, without reference to conflict of law principles), exclusive jurisdiction and venue in state or federal courts located in Santa Clara County, California, and a waiver of jury trial. The agreement provides for injunctive or equitable relief in the event of unauthorized disclosure, clarifies that all Confidential Information remains the property of the Disclosing Party, and states that no express or implied rights or licenses are granted. It includes standard clauses on independent development, compliance with applicable laws, entire agreement, amendment only by written instrument signed by authorized representatives, non-waiver, severability, binding effect on successors and lawful assigns, and assignment restrictions (with exceptions for merger, reorganization, consolidation, change of control, or sale of substantially all assets). Either party may terminate with 30 days’ prior written notice, with confidentiality obligations surviving termination.

Use this document when a prospect asks for “your NDA,” “CommerceIQ standard mutual NDA,” “CIQ NDA template,” or when legal review is required before sharing sensitive product information, pricing models, customer data, technical architecture, or roadmap details. It is the correct template for early-stage sales cycles, partnership evaluations, and pre-contract due diligence discussions.

Not to confuse with: (1) a Customer Master Services Agreement (MSA), which governs paid commercial terms and service delivery; (2) a Data Processing Agreement (DPA), which addresses personal data and regulatory compliance; or (3) a Unilateral NDA, where only one party discloses confidential information. This document is specifically a mutual, reciprocal NDA designed for balanced two-way information exchange.

Version information is not explicitly listed in the sample content; the document appears to be an active standard template for Sales/BD use. Effective date is determined upon execution by the parties, as reflected in the signature block.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Shelf Agent Training - a sales enablement guide that explains what AllyAI Shelf Agent is, how it differs from Content Agent, what data it uses (DSO vs PIM), and how to position it in market. An enablement guide is used internally to train sales, GTM, and agency teams on product positioning, use cases, differentiators, and outcomes. This document is designed to help teams confidently explain Shelf Agent’s value, articulate the separation from Content Agent, and sell Shelf Agent & Services as part of the CommerceIQ AI Platform.

The document defines AllyAI Shelf Agent as being built on DSO (Digital Shelf Optimization) data and analyzing content, availability, assortment, ratings, and search signals. It explains that Shelf Agent detects what is driving digital shelf performance, delivers prioritized next best actions, and generates executive-ready Insight Packs. Core outcomes highlighted include: creating business reports in less than 10 minutes, increasing shelf scores by 10+ points, driving retail readiness across CAARS, and producing 500+ shelf insight packs globally in minutes (Coke example). The document emphasizes automated reporting, digital shelf insights, and side-by-side comparisons showing that while agencies report scores, Shelf Agent recommends actions to improve them.

A major section explains the strategic separation of Shelf Agent from Content Agent under the theme: “Different Use Cases. Different Data. Different Agents.” Shelf Agent is built on DSO data (content, availability, ratings, search), while Content Agent is built on PIM and PDP content data and focuses on compliance and optimization. Content Agent capabilities include detecting content gaps and compliance issues, optimizing titles/bullets/images/attributes, syndicating updates to retailers and back to PIM, achieving +10 PIM compliance points in less than 2 weeks, 90%+ PIM compliance across retailers, and reducing time to action to less than 1 minute (vs 35-minute industry average). The training also situates Shelf Agent within the broader CommerceIQ AI Platform, alongside Sales Agent, Media Agent, Inventory Agent, Retail Context Engine, and associated Services, and references the 2025 (Software Budgets) to 2026 (Agency Budgets) evolution with positioning such as “More features, Lower Price.”

The document includes positioning statements such as “Create business reports in minutes,” “Increase shelf scores 10+ points,” and “Drive retail readiness across the shelf.” It references a global Coca-Cola use case (33 countries, 355 retailers, thousands of SKUs) where regional teams need timely insight to impact digital shelf score, illustrating scalability and automation value. It also references supporting assets in development (Shelf Agent Pitch Deck, Demo Script, Datasheet, Messaging Doc) and resource locations (Landing page, Product Box – DSO, Product Box – Shelf Agent, GTM Enablement > AllyAI > Shelf Agent).

This is the Profitero Competitive Battle Card_101525 (Updated Oct 2025) – a sales battle card designed to equip CommerceIQ account executives, BDRs, and sales leaders to win against Profitero in competitive opportunities. A battle card is a tactical sales enablement document that provides competitive intelligence, objection handling, positioning guidance, pricing insights, and targeted discovery questions. This document is specifically used in live deals where Profitero is the incumbent or a shortlisted competitor.

The document outlines where Profitero competes directly with CommerceIQ products, including Digital Shelf 360 (DS including B&M), Amazon Market Share (Sales & Share), Shelf Intelligent Retail Media & Shelf Intelligent Analytics (via integrations with Pacvue, Skai, or Publicis), and Profitero Copilot (via Salsify integration for ESM & PRA). It details Profitero’s pricing structure (DS charged by SKU per retailer tier – Tier 1 up to 3,000 SKUs, Tier 2 up to 2,000, Tier 3 up to 1,000; MS charged on performance, meaning more sales = higher client cost). It includes competitive intelligence such as Publicis ownership, Publicis sales goals tied to Profitero, discounted “family rates” (~30% cheaper for Publicis clients), and the constraint that CIQ cannot pitch with Publicis unless the client explicitly rejects Profitero.

The battle card breaks down “Why They Win” (Integrated Digital Shelf + Market Share platform, Open Commerce Ecosystem, competitive benchmarking focus, strong professional services, trusted ownership by Publicis) versus “Why They Lose” (complex UI and navigation, over-reliance on third-party integrations, limited retailer media coverage, limited mobile app coverage, inflexible data refresh rates, SKU maintenance challenges, data quality and actionability concerns). It cites discovery insights from Glanbia (SKU maintenance challenges, 11/28 call) and WGS RFP (data quality concerns). It also highlights specific feature gaps such as availability only showing the last day of a time range, dashboard views limited to top 6 brands on page 1, promotion visibility limited to discount % without full promo detail, and potential limitations in global retailer coverage.

The document reinforces CIQ differentiation with quantified proof points: 1,450+ retailers across 85+ countries, 100+ mobile apps covered, 90% data accuracy via Transparency Dashboard, data refresh up to 6x daily (top SKUs up to 24x), 530M products in database, ~55M new products added per quarter, 200 unique attributes captured, 4,000+ brands, 8,000+ retailers, 50+ countries supported, and 7 global offices (Boston, NYC, Dublin, London, Shanghai, Tokyo, Minsk). It includes digital shelf performance statistics used in selling: 42% sales loss when OOS drops below 30%, +86% sales lift from top 10 search placement, 206% sales lift from increasing review velocity from 1–5% to 5–10% monthly, 58% lift from improved content, and 11% sales loss when losing Buy Box due to price.

Use this document when someone asks: “How do we position against Profitero?”, “What are Profitero’s weaknesses?”, “How does Profitero price Digital Shelf?”, “What’s the impact of Publicis owning Profitero?”, “How does CIQ compare on retailer coverage or refresh rates?”, or “What FUD questions should we ask in a Profitero deal?”

This is specifically a tactical, deal-focused competitive displacement tool.

A battle card is a tactical sales enablement document used in live deals to understand a competitor’s positioning, strengths, weaknesses, pricing, customers, and how to respond. documents.name: Comprehensive Prime Day Report July 2024
documents.documentIdentity: This is the Comprehensive Prime Day Report July 2024 - a data-driven industry performance recap analyzing traffic, conversion, inventory, advertising spend, discounting strategies, CPCs, ROAS, and revenue impact during Prime Day 2024 (July 16–17) compared to the prior 28-day baseline (L28) and year-over-year versus 2023, using CommerceIQ REM Platform internal data.
documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Comprehensive Prime Day Report July 2024 - a detailed post-event performance analysis built from CommerceIQ’s REM Platform data, covering Prime Day activity from 12:00AM PST July 16 through 11:59PM PST July 17, 2024, benchmarked against the prior 28-day (L28) average and compared year-over-year to 2023. As an enablement guide, this document equips sales, customer success, and strategy teams with data-backed insights to advise brands on discounting, inventory planning, ad spend allocation, and post-event optimization strategies.

The report analyzes traffic, conversion, and revenue dynamics during Prime Day 2024. It shows traffic spiked by +59% over baseline in 2024 vs. 2023, with mid-range discounts (10%–20%) generating the strongest traffic lift—correlating with 10x to 15x increases in glance views versus L28 averages. However, the increase in traffic did not directly translate into revenue growth due to declining unit conversion rates during the event, which took 5–7 days post-event to recover. Conversion rates dropped on Day 1 and remained depressed until a week after Prime Day ended.

A major focus of the report is inventory performance and out-of-stocks (OOS). Revenue loss due to OOS spiked significantly in 2024, in some analyses showing +200% vs. 2023 and in certain category cuts up to +1000% vs. 2023. Categories such as Toys, Home & Kitchen, and Beauty experienced heavy revenue losses when increased traffic hit OOS PDPs. The report contrasts sections showing both poor inventory planning (with 10x spikes in OOS losses) and areas where brands improved planning, halving the impact of OOS losses versus 2023. The key insight: insufficient inventory during peak traffic was one of the most costly Prime Day execution gaps.

Advertising strategy and efficiency are examined in depth. Brands increased ad spend significantly during Prime Day—up to 100–150% more than 2023 in some industry cuts—with Sponsored Display spend increasing up to 10x relative to baseline and other ad types increasing 4x+. Sponsored Product and Sponsored Display gained share in 2024, whereas Sponsored Brand had been the primary focus in 2023. CPCs rose (2x increase going into Day 2), contributing to ROAS declines on Day 2. Overall ROAS was strong relative to baseline except for Day 2, and ROAS performed best at minimal discounts (<5%) or moderate 10%–20% discounts. Post-event, brands pulled back ad spend by upwards of 40%, with most ad types declining sharply except Sponsored Display, which remained elevated up to 7 days post-event in some categories. ASPs declined and discounting levels were generally lower relative to baseline than the prior year.

Use this document when someone asks: “What happened during Prime Day 2024?”, “How did traffic and conversion perform?”, “What discount level drove the most glance views?”, “How much did OOS cost brands?”, “What happened to ROAS and CPCs?”, “How did ad spend shift between Sponsored Brand, Sponsored Product, and Sponsored Display?”, or “How should we plan inventory and ads for the next Prime event?”

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the CommerceIQ-Prime-Big-Deal-Days-2025-Report - a detailed sales enablement performance report analyzing Prime Day 2025 results versus 2024 and versus the L14 (last 14-day) baseline average. As an enablement guide, this document equips sales, customer success, and retail media teams with data-driven insights to discuss Prime Day outcomes, category-level performance shifts, advertising efficiency, and inventory impact using CommerceIQ’s REM Platform data. It is used to support strategic conversations with brands following major tentpole events like Prime Day.

The report covers Prime Day 2025 performance from 12:00AM PST to 11:59PM PST on July 8 and July 11, 2025, benchmarked against the prior 14-day average. It analyzes Gross Margin (including a 31% YoY drop overall and 13% YoY decline in certain segments), Ordered Revenue (including a 60% YoY decline in Toys and 32% YoY growth in Health & Personal Care), Glance Views (20% YoY decrease overall, but +369% Day 1 spike in Beauty), Unit Conversion (447% YoY drop in some segments; 112% YoY decline in Beauty), and Revenue Loss Due to Out-of-Stock (27% YoY increase in some categories). The document repeatedly contrasts Day 1 vs Day 2 performance shifts, highlighting changing consumer behavior and advertising strategies.

Category-level deep dives include Beauty (3× baseline revenue momentum but -3% YoY; 81% gross margin improvement despite being negative YoY), Tools & Home Improvement (34% gross margin decrease but 12.51% ROAS increase), Health & Personal Care (9% gross margin decline and 34.14% ROAS drop despite 32% revenue growth), Grocery (-21% YoY revenue with improved OOS discipline), Patio, Lawn & Garden (strong YoY revenue lift but heavy OOS losses), and Toys (60% YoY revenue drop with Day 2 outperforming Day 1). The report also details ad performance shifts, including a 3–5% YoY increase in ad spend, total ROAS declining by 233% overall, Sponsored Display surging +814% on Day 1 in 2025 vs +27% in 2024, and CPC inflation driving margin pressure.

The document emphasizes key structural themes: traffic volatility, conversion inefficiencies, CPC inflation, smarter bidding strategies, upper-funnel investment shifts, and the material impact of inventory discipline. It positions CommerceIQ’s REM Platform as capable of real-time margin protection and performance optimization during high-velocity events.

Use this document when someone asks: “How did Prime Day 2025 perform vs 2024?”, “What happened to ROAS during Prime Day?”, “Which categories won or lost on Prime Day 2025?”, “How did OOS impact revenue?”, “What drove gross margin decline?”, or “How did Sponsored Display perform during Prime Day?” It is particularly valuable for post-event business reviews (EBRs/QBRs) and strategic upsell discussions around media optimization and inventory planning.

The document positions Shelf Agent as an AI-powered intelligence layer built on top of Digital Shelf Optimization (DSO) data. It explains that Shelf Agent eliminates manual reporting cycles by using conversational workflows powered by Ask AllyAI and automated insight generation to turn weeks of analysis into seconds. Core capabilities include plain-language interrogation of DSO data, automated drill-down analysis without manual dashboard navigation, and generation of executive-ready Insight Packs. These Insight Packs are configurable by brand, retailer, market, category, SKU, and timeframe (weekly, monthly, quarterly, or ad hoc) and include executive summaries, key performance drivers, prioritized actions, and export-ready PowerPoint outputs in brand-approved templates.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the CommerceIQ-CategoryIQ-Hair-Styling-April-2025 - a CategoryIQ market intelligence report that unpacks US Amazon category-level data for Hair Styling products. An enablement guide of this type is used by sales and customer success teams to educate brands on category trends, competitive dynamics, and growth levers across ecommerce P&L metrics (sales, traffic, conversion, ASP, share of voice, content quality, and promotional strategy). It is designed to support strategic conversations with brand partners and prospects by grounding recommendations in concrete data.

The report opens with an Executive Summary and Category Overview highlighting that the Hair Products: Hair Styling: Others category grew 23% year-over-year, from $96.3M to $118.4M (Dec 29, 2024–Mar 22, 2025 vs prior year), outperforming adjacent Personal Care categories that grew on average 16%. It also references broader category growth, including Hair Color: Powder (+51.1%, from $5.7M to $8.6M) and Body Wash: Liquid (+15.1%, from $114.5M to $131.8M). The document emphasizes that Sponsored Share of Voice (SOV) acts as a proxy for ad spend and that alignment between paid and organic presence is critical to conversion and sustained market share.

A deep competitive section analyzes brands such as Color Wow (market share up from 3.7% to 4.5%, sales up 49% from $2.3M to $5.5M), Moroccanoil (ASP increased from $25.64 to $25.74), and Amika (paid presence up 1.1% while organic declined 0.4%). It tracks organic vs paid SOV shifts (e.g., Color Wow organic down 2.2% and paid down 1.6%) and benchmarks brands across Ecommerce P&L drivers: Sales, Traffic, Conversion, ASP, Brand Strength, Share of Voice, Assortment Strength, Content Quality, Out of Stock Rate, Consumer Sentiment, Pricing, and Promotional Strategy. The report also includes competitive benchmarking tables and highlights top gainers and losers.

Search and assortment insights show that Curl Defining Cream (1.65% SOV) and Edge Control (1.6% SOV) are top searched themes, with Hair Wax and Hair Styling Mousse representing a combined 2.5% SOV among top themes. Hair Volumizing leads with 6.6% category share, and three of the top six buying themes relate to volume (15.5% combined). Garnier accounts for 12% of category search. The Anti Frizz theme shows Revlon holding 18.3% share, and Hair Volumizing shows I Dew Care at 10.4%, signaling whitespace opportunities. Pricing analysis reveals that $7–$11 (22.5%) and $12–$16 (21%) price bands together drive 44% of units, while the $22–$26 band contributes 15% of units but 20.4% of revenue. Premium tail bands ($42–$46 and >$49) account for 2.6% of units and 7.7% of revenue.

For the Content Agent Pitch, reps must walk through the AI Shelf story, explain the challenge of keeping content optimized and PIM compliant, define what AllyAI Content Agent is, present the Newell customer story, and then perform a live demo.

The Content Agent Demo section provides a required demo flow: start with a strong hook reiterating the content challenge; show how the platform prioritizes which SKUs to fix; demonstrate how it evaluates PIM and PDP content; review the reasoning behind suggested improvements; demo accepting a change and publishing it; and close by summarizing the outcomes delivered. This is the Product Box: AllyAI SalesAgent & Services – a structured product definition document that clearly articulates what the AllyAI Sales Agent is, what it includes, and how it delivers value. A Product Box is used in sales enablement to define a product’s scope, positioning, core capabilities, supported retailers, add-on services, and differentiators in one consolidated reference. This document is used by sales, customer success, and leadership teams to understand what is in scope, how it works, where it is available, and how it should be positioned in customer conversations.

The document defines the Sales Agent as an AI-powered commerce analyst built on Amazon Vendor Central data, currently available for Amazon across the US, Canada, EU5, and Australia, with expanded PRA support in the US, EU9, Brazil, Mexico, and Australia. It clarifies regional feature limitations (e.g., specific chargeback and shortage restrictions in markets like the Netherlands or Poland). It explains key AI skills, including Ask AllyAI (conversational analytics for plain-language queries), Gap to Plan (measures pacing vs. targets and recommends actions across media, content, and availability), Automated Deck Creation (one-click PowerPoint exports with GenAI-driven insights), and Ask AllyAI Diagnostics (Deep Reasoning engine launching end of Q1 that explains why trends occurred and prescribes corrective actions). It also distinguishes between Ask Ally (what happened) and Sales Diagnostics (why it happened and what to do next).

A major section covers gap closure frameworks across four dimensions: Media Gap Closure (reallocating spend from low-performing SKUs and estimating incremental investment needed), Content Compliance Gap Closure (PIM and retailer requirement mismatches prioritized by revenue impact), Content Efficacy Gap Closure (AI-driven competitive listing and semantic analysis to improve organic rank and conversion), and Availability Gap Closure (stockout forecasting with SKU- and store-level signals). The document also details retail financial reconciliation capabilities through Profit Recovery Automation (PRA), including Deductions Overview, Price Variance (PPV), Shortages (PQV), Chargebacks, Shipment Tracker, and Invoice Journey Maps that track Phase 1 and Phase 2 dispute recovery.

Additionally, it outlines retail content protection automations such as Unauthorized ASIN detection (automatic Amazon ticket submission to remove duplicate listings), Content Authority automation (restores unauthorized title/bullet/description edits), and Variation Authority automation (merges orphaned 1P variants under a parent ASIN). The document includes Custom Agent Branding (customers can rename and visually brand the agent), Self-Serve Agent Training (add custom business context), Interactive RCA Refinement, and Retailer Copilot references. It also references Agency Services (ExpertIQ) that leverage Sales Agent data for managed services support. documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the CommerceIQ-CategoryIQ-Liquid-Body-Wash-April-2025 - a CategoryIQ quarterly e-commerce performance report focused on the US Amazon Liquid Body Wash category. An enablement guide of this type is a data-driven category deep dive used by sales, account management, and retail media teams to educate brand partners on market dynamics, competitive shifts, and actionable growth levers. It is typically used in business reviews, strategic planning sessions, and prospect conversations to demonstrate CommerceIQ’s analytics capabilities and category expertise.

The report covers year-over-year growth trends (Dec 29, 2024 to Mar 22, 2025 vs. Dec 29, 2023 to Mar 22, 2024), highlighting that the Liquid Body Wash category grew 15.1% from $114.5M to $131.8M, outperforming several adjacent segments. It benchmarks related categories such as Hair Color: Powder (+51.1%, from $5.7M to $8.6M) and Hair Styling: Others (+23%, from $96.3M to $118.4M), noting that similar categories grew on average 16%. The executive summary identifies three key insights: (1) the $5–$14 price range drives 60% of unit sales, (2) lower-priced products dominate the digital shelf, and (3) promotions are a primary growth driver.

A significant portion of the document focuses on pricing architecture and promotional strategy. The $5–$9 band alone contributes 30.5% of units (23% of revenue), while $10–$14 contributes 29.5% of units. Tail price bands ($35–$39, $40–$44, and >$48) represent only 1.5% of units but 4.6% of revenue. The report shows that Dove increased promotion by 29.9% (from 0.03% to 29.9%) and gained market share from 16.3% to 18.4% (+12.9% growth). Olay reduced ASP by 40%, driving a 50%+ sales increase to $5.5M with only a 3.6% promotion increase. Method and Aveeno also scaled promotions (Method to 3.5%, Aveeno to 11.7%). The analysis ties promotion rate changes directly to market share gains and ROAS considerations.

The report also dives into traffic drivers, including Sponsored Share of Voice (SOV) as a proxy for ad spend, organic vs paid presence, and search behavior themes. For example, Dove’s paid presence decline resulted in a 5.5% share drop in one view, signaling opportunity for competitors. Theme analysis shows "Moisturizing Skin Care" at 25.5% share, "Paraben Free Products" at 9% SOV, and "Gel Cleanse" at 11.5%. In the Paraben Free segment, Dove dominates with 69.4% share, while the Paraben Chemicals theme is more contested (Native 25.8%, Salt Stone 24.4%, top 3 holding 50.2%). Search themes such as "Body Wash For Men" (3.1%) and "Women’s Body Wash" (2.3%) are analyzed, with brands like Method (8.6%) and Nivea Men (7.3%) leading in men’s queries. The document also references ecommerce P&L drivers including Sales, Traffic, Conversion, ASP, Share of Voice, Assortment Strength, Out of Stock Rate, Consumer Sentiment, Content Quality, Pricing, and Promotional Strategy.

Use this document if someone asks: “What’s happening in the Amazon Liquid Body Wash category?”, “How is Dove winning share?”, “What price bands drive the most unit volume?”, “How are promotions impacting market share?”, “What’s the opportunity in Paraben-Free body wash?”, or “How should we benchmark our brand vs Dove, Olay, or Method?” It is especially useful for quarterly business reviews (QBRs), category strategy discussions, and retail media investment planning.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the IndustryTrends-TheStateofRetailEcomm-Q3 - a Q3 2024 retail ecommerce industry trends report built from aggregated internal data from CommerceIQ’s REM Platform for Amazon sellers (April 2023 to September 2024). As an enablement guide, this document equips sales, strategy, and customer teams with data-backed market context to support conversations with brands. It is used to demonstrate macro ecommerce shifts, benchmark performance, and frame strategic recommendations around advertising, pricing, inventory, and operational efficiency.

The report includes a Total Industry Overview and multiple category deep dives: Beauty, Tools & Home, Health & Personal Care, Grocery, Toys, and an “Others” category. Core performance lenses include Ad Spend | ROAS | CPC; On-Hand Inventory; Revenue Loss Due to Out-of-Stocks (RepOOS); OPS vs. Unit Margin %; Price Level vs. Discount %; Fulfillment and Fill Rates; Glance Views; and Revenue trends. It compares Q3 2023 vs. Q3 2024 and highlights QoQ shifts within 2024, especially around tentpole moments like Prime Day.

Specific insights include: CPC remaining relatively flat YoY despite volatile ad spend; a projected Q4 2024 increase in ad spend with expected ROAS compression; ad spend increasing 20% YoY in Tools & Home while declining 9.7% QoQ post-events; ROAS increasing 53.5% to $7.32 during off-peak periods as ad spend declined; unit margins declining from 37% to 35.8% in Beauty alongside a -1% YoY price change; Tools & Home unit margins down 740 basis points QoQ; Grocery prices remaining stable over 18 months with reduced discounting in H2 2024; on-hand inventory rising 15% YoY in Tools & Home and 25% YoY in Health & Personal Care; Toys inventory peaking at 54% higher YoY in September; overall on-hand inventory in “Others” declining 17% YoY; RepOOS peaking at 2.5% in August vs. a ~2% benchmark; and fulfilled units in Tools & Home declining 17% YoY while fill rates stayed flat.

The document also emphasizes macro themes: rising COGS squeezing margins despite stable pricing, declining advertising efficiency due to mix shift toward lower ASP products, improved operational efficiency with record-high fill rates, and tentpole events driving spikes in glance views and seasonal out-of-stocks. It highlights that many sales spikes were driven by organic traffic rather than incremental ad spend, especially during holiday peaks.

This is the CommerceIQ-Prime-Day-2024-Insights - a detailed event recap and analytics report summarizing Prime Day 2024 performance across multiple retail categories using CommerceIQ’s REM Platform data. The document analyzes ordered revenue and Average Selling Price (ASP) changes by hour during Prime Day (July 16–17, 2024), benchmarking performance against the L6 Day Average (July 10–15, 2024). It includes hourly performance charts (12:00AM–11:59PM PST), percent change in ordered revenue vs. baseline, percent change in ASP vs. baseline, and comparisons of hourly revenue distribution between Prime Day 2023 and 2024. documents.documentIdentity: This is the CommerceIQ Copy & Content Style Guide (CommerceIQ-ContentStyleGuide.pdf) - a comprehensive brand writing standards manual that defines CommerceIQ’s brand voice, editorial hierarchy, grammar and punctuation rules, capitalization standards, industry naming conventions, digital asset requirements, and approved terminology for all customer-facing and internal marketing content.
documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the CommerceIQ Copy & Content Style Guide (CommerceIQ-ContentStyleGuide.pdf) - a comprehensive brand writing standards manual that defines how CommerceIQ communicates across all written content. As an enablement guide, it establishes the rules, tone, hierarchy and technical conventions that marketing, sales, BDRs, executives and content contributors must follow to ensure consistency across website copy, decks, emails, press releases, social media and sales materials. It serves as the single source of truth for writing style across the CommerceIQ brand.

The document is structured into clear sections: About CommerceIQ (company boilerplate and positioning), Our Brand Voice, General Style Notes, Technical Style Notes, Notes on Digital Assets, and Style Guide Exceptions. It includes the official company boilerplate describing CommerceIQ as an AI-powered digital commerce platform with a global network of 900+ retailers serving 2,200+ leading brands. The Brand Voice section defines five pillars: About them, not us; Expert & insightful; Inclusive, empathetic & relatable; Clear & concise; and Trustworthy, familiar & personal. It explicitly mandates avoiding passive voice, prioritizing clarity (“Say what you mean”), eliminating jargon, and focusing messaging on customer outcomes rather than company promotion.

The Technical Style Notes section defines a strict hierarchy of style: (1) CommerceIQ style, (2) AP style, (3) Editor’s discretion. It outlines headline formatting rules (sentence case except press releases; all-caps eyebrows; capitalize first word after a colon; no periods in headlines; use “&” instead of “and” in headlines), capitalization rules (default to sentence case; brands treated as singular nouns; capitalize only proper nouns and product names), and punctuation standards (no Oxford comma unless necessary; space before and after ellipses; no spaces around em dashes; double quotation marks only; exclamation points used sparingly). It mandates contractions (you’ll, we’ll, it’s), spells out numbers less than 10 in body copy (AP style), and defines usage rules for abbreviations and acronyms (cite on first reference, avoid internal acronyms like “CIQ” in public-facing content). It includes preferred spellings such as ecommerce (lowercase), return on ad spend (ROAS), cost per click (CPC), iROAS, eBook, am/pm (lowercase, no periods), and ET/PT for time zones.

The guide also standardizes industry category capitalization (e.g., Beauty & Personal Care, Grocery & Gourmet Food, Sports & Outdoors, Tools & Home Improvement) and enforces the use of “&” in category names. The report covers Ordered Product Sales (OPS), unit margins, ad spend, ROAS, CPC, inventory levels, fulfillment metrics, out-of-stock (OOS) revenue loss, pricing and discount trends, glance views, and conversion rates across industries including Health & Personal Care, Pet Products, Tools & Home, Beauty, Furniture, Grocery, Toys, Office Products, and Patio, Lawn & Garden.
documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the CommerceIQ “The State of Retail Ecommerce: Q3 2025” Report (September version) – a quarterly ecommerce performance and insights report built from aggregated internal data from CommerceIQ’s Retail Ecommerce Management (REM) Platform for Amazon users. An enablement guide of this type is used by sales, customer success, marketing, and strategy teams to educate prospects and customers on macro ecommerce trends, category benchmarks, and performance shifts. It is best used in strategic conversations, QBRs, and executive discussions where industry context and data-backed insights are required.

The report provides a Q3 2025 vs. Q3 2024 year-over-year analysis across multiple retail categories. Core performance metrics include Ordered Product Sales (OPS) vs. Unit Margin %, Ad Spend | ROAS | CPC, Revenue Loss Due to Out-of-Stock (OOS), On-Hand Inventory, Fulfillment (PO Fill Rate, Filled Units), Price Level vs. Discount %, Glance Views, and Conversion Rates. For example, in Health & Personal Care, Q3 OPS increased 13.88% while unit margins declined 2.17% in July (likely driven by Prime Day promotions). Ad spend in this category grew 33% YoY, CPC rose 11.6%, and ROAS declined 17.6%. Fill rate climbed to a 91% 18-month high, and filled units increased 9.32% YoY. Glance views rose 22.4% YoY while conversions declined 1.1%.

The Pet Products category showed improved efficiency, with ad spend up 14.9% YoY, ROAS increasing 22.1% YoY, and CPC declining 10.2% YoY due to improved conversion and keyword diversification. However, revenue loss from OOS more than doubled at 139% YoY. In Tools & Home, OPS declined 6.7% YoY and gross margin decreased 0.9%, while ad spend surged 47.6% YoY, CPC rose 14.5%, and ROAS declined 16.2%. Revenue loss from OOS increased 1.9% YoY despite a 2.8% decline in OOS percentage.

Additional category highlights include: Beauty (on-hand inventory up 3.3% YoY; PO Fill Rate up 5.4% YoY; discounts down 1.6% while ASP declined 2.1%), Furniture (OPS down 24% YoY in one view; inventory down 52% YoY; PO Fill Rate up 26.5%; ASP up 0.7%; discounts down 3.8%; glance views down 29.5% while conversion increased 0.2%), Grocery (revenue lost due to OOS up 108% YoY despite improved fill rates), Office Products (ad spend down 1.1%; CPC down 11.1%; ROAS up 1.5%; revenue loss due to OOS down 62% YoY), and Toys (revenue lost due to OOS down 31% YoY). The report consistently ties performance shifts to tentpole events like Prime Day and competitive CPC pressure.

Use this report when someone asks: “What happened in ecommerce in Q3 2025?”, “How did Prime Day impact margins and OPS?”, “What are the latest Amazon CPC and ROAS trends?”, “How are different categories performing YoY?”, or “What’s the impact of OOS on revenue this quarter?” It is ideal for data-backed storytelling in prospect meetings, QBRs, industry webinars, and executive briefings.

Not to confuse with: a product datasheet (which explains CommerceIQ platform features), a sales deck (which pitches REM capabilities and pricing), or a case study (which highlights a single customer’s results). This report is macro-level, multi-category, and insight-driven rather than product-feature focused.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Content Agent Training Deck - a product training and go-to-market enablement presentation designed to educate internal teams (CSDs, sales, FDEs, marketing, and enablement) on CommerceIQ’s Content Agent, its positioning within the broader AI agent strategy, and how to drive customer deployment by end of Q1 2026. A training deck is an internal-facing document used to align teams on product vision, capabilities, customer value, implementation requirements, and sales motion. This deck is intended to prepare teams to launch, position, and deploy Content Agent across the DSO (Digital Shelf Optimization) and Copilot customer base.

The deck begins with the strategic vision: CommerceIQ’s pivot from data & analytics (Digital Shelf, Market Share, RMM, Copilot) toward automation through AI Agents (Content Agent, Sales Agent, Media Agent, Stock Agent). It outlines the market reality driving this shift—data commoditization, manual workflows, and increasing margin pressure. It introduces the concept of "Retail AI Agents" and positions Content Agent as part of Ally AI Teammates, moving the company from 80% data / 20% services (2024–25) to 60% automation-led solutions by 2026+.

A core section details the Digital Content Workflow Challenge: brands manage 6,000+ SKUs on Amazon US alone, spend 30–35 minutes per SKU identifying and fixing content gaps across 5+ systems, and lack clear prioritization between Copilot and Digital Shelf Agent (DSA). The deck highlights current product gaps: no easy prioritization of content gaps in CIQ Digital Shelf, Copilot limited to copy-based actionability, no visibility when PIM is the source of gaps, and manual, ad hoc identification of PDP vs Gold Standard compliance issues. It introduces Content Agent’s capabilities: retailer-specific content augmentation, automated PDP indexing optimization, 1-click syndication to retail partners (Amazon, Walmart, Kroger, Costco), brand-context training via natural language inputs, two-way PIM integration, custom scoring logic, and dashboards for PIM-PDP compliance.

The deck includes a detailed Newell case study: 29 joint meetings post-September 25 kickoff; collaboration across 2 AI Outcome Managers, 3 UI Designers, 12 Engineers, 3 Omni Enablement, 2 Digital Merchandising, and 1 Salsify partner. Within 60 days, 75 SKUs achieved 100% PIM compliance; 80 SKUs aligned within 1 hour; time to action reduced from ~30+ minutes per SKU to <1 minute (or ~5 minutes including workflow triggers). It references a remaining 9 SKU gap and reports results to CEO within 80 days. It also details Forward Deployment Engineer (FDE) workflow: stakeholder onboarding, capturing brand-specific content logic, collecting business context, building two-way PIM integration, and developing custom scoring thresholds. Additional sections cover macro, retailer, category, brand, and persona context inputs (e.g., Amazon image suppression rules, Walmart shorter title ranking, pet food protein trends, EU sustainability guidelines), brand guardrails (phrasing restrictions like avoiding “Made in USA” on Amazon), and internal change management requirements.

The GTM and offer structure is clearly defined: Content Agent is free for 1 retailer (in 1 market) and 1 brand in 1 category for the life of the existing contract; preferred PIM is Salsify; no order form change required; retailer eligibility limited to Amazon, Walmart, Kroger, Costco due to automated syndication capabilities. The deck includes a Customer GTM schedule (email announcements, webinar invites, recap, “don’t miss out” email, deployment start dates such as 12/15, 1/13, 2/2), and a stated goal: 100% of DSO & Copilot customers deploy 1 Content Agent by end of Q1 2026, requiring sign-up by end of January 2026.

Use this document if someone asks: “What is Content Agent and how does it work?”, “How do we position Content Agent to DSO/Copilot customers?”, “What’s the Newell case study?”, “What does implementation require from a brand?”, “What is the free offer structure?”, or “What is our Q1 deployment goal?” It is particularly useful for internal training, QBR preparation, stakeholder alignment, and early access rollout planning.

Not to confuse with: a Content Agent One-Pager (external high-level summary), a Sales Agent Product Box (formal product definition and pricing structure), a Second Call Deck (customer-facing deep sales presentation), or a Battle Card (competitive positioning). This deck is broader—covering strategy, implementation, GTM motion, and enablement.

A battlecard is a sales enablement document used during competitive deals to quickly articulate strengths, weaknesses, and positioning versus named competitors. This document is specifically focused on CommerceIQ’s Retail Media Management (RMM) solution and how it outperforms Skai, Profitero, Pacvue, Flywheel, and Tinuiti.

The document is structured by core capability areas including Share of Voice (SOV) Optimization, Budget Optimization, Incrementality, Shelf-Aware Advertising, and Unified Retail Data Integration. It details CommerceIQ’s ability to scrape and track 4,000+ keywords daily covering >80% of category sales, provide weighted SOV (giving more value to higher placements), track item-level SOV, and fully integrate SOV signals into automated bidding and budget actions. In contrast, competitors are shown to have limitations such as unweighted SOV (Skai), limited keyword quotas of only several hundred terms (Pacvue), manual SOV usage not tied to automation, or reliance on integrations like Profitero for competitive metrics.

In Budget Optimization, the document highlights CommerceIQ’s automated budget pacing, mid-month budget adjustment capabilities, day-of-week optimization, and the ability to over-index spend during key retail events like Prime Day. Competitor gaps include manual budget pacing (Flywheel), insights without automated activation (Skai), and reliance on managed services partnerships rather than in-platform tech (Profitero). In Incrementality, CommerceIQ’s AI-based model standardizes ROI using iROAS (Incremental Return on Ad Spend) and incorporates SOV, search rankings, shopper propensity, and relevancy signals. Tinuiti is positioned as relying on traditional Amazon metrics like TACoS and manual branded keyword testing, while others lack a comparable incrementality model or rely on experimental hubs rather than integrated AI optimization.

The document also emphasizes Shelf-Aware Advertising and flexible automations, including full retail data integration into ad optimization (on-hand and open PO inventory, competitive mapping, elasticity modeling, inventory- and profit-aware bidding). Competitor limitations include partial retail data integration, lack of inventory-aware automation, no hourly bidder (Flywheel), lack of item-level nuance for Walmart 3P sellers (Skai), and required third-party integrations (Profitero, Pacvue). Embedded throughout are FUD-based discovery questions sales reps can use to expose weaknesses in competitor solutions—covering pacing concerns, incrementality measurement gaps, data silos, lack of AI automation, and limited SOV visibility.

Use this document when a prospect mentions Skai, Pacvue, Profitero, Flywheel, or Tinuiti; when preparing for a competitive deal; when asked about SOV automation, incrementality modeling, Prime Day budget strategies, or inventory-aware advertising; or when a rep needs targeted FUD questions for discovery. It is especially useful in late-stage deals where differentiation on automation depth and AI sophistication matters.

Not to confuse with the RMM Second Call Deck (which provides a structured customer-facing presentation), the RMM First Call Deck (high-level overview), or a Product Box (which defines positioning, pricing, and packaging). This document is tactical and competitive in nature, meant for internal sales enablement rather than external presentation.
