documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the ExpertIQ Training Deck Internal - an internal-facing sales and enablement presentation designed to train Account Executives (AEs), Customer Success, and Product Success teams on how to position, sell, and deliver ExpertIQ Insights & Advisory services. A training deck is an internal education tool that explains product positioning, service structure, pricing, use cases, and sales process guidance. This deck is specifically used to help revenue teams articulate the value of ExpertIQ beyond in-product dashboards and AllyAI 1-click reports, and to drive adoption, upsells, and long-term service stickiness.

The deck defines what ExpertIQ is: advanced insights and advisory services that go beyond self-serve dashboards, providing bespoke briefs, custom analytics, and strategic recommendations. It introduces the core Job-To-Be-Done (JTBD): "When I’m overwhelmed by ecommerce data, I want expert guidance that transforms raw data into actionable strategies so I can confidently prioritize initiatives that drive measurable business outcomes." It explains the service ecosystem: foundational Customer Success at onboarding, Product Success for incremental enablement and best practices, and ExpertIQ for deep analytics and advisory. It emphasizes partnership (consistent global point of contact), global expertise across markets and categories, and the Plan / Do / Review cycle with analysis and action planning.

The content includes detailed examples of analytics capabilities such as Amazon Marketing Cloud (AMC) Exposure Overlap Analysis (demonstrating DSP as first touchpoint and Search as final conversion driver), RFMD shopper segmentation (Recency, Frequency, Monetary, Diversity), shopper cohorting (Champion, Potential Champion, Need Attention, Lost Champion, About to Churn), and Share of Search analysis across paid and organic. Sample data points include: 42% of generic search terms captured by Brand A, 31% organic share vs 19% for Competitor 2 (12% gap), paid search gaps of 3–4%, >50% share terms across categories like "chocolate bar" and "share pack," 6% Champion shoppers vs 10% Potential Champions, and 75% of repeat buyers concentrated in 10 SKUs. It also includes promotional analysis (8 vs 9–10 products on promotion, 15–40% competitor discount ranges vs 20–30% for Brand A, average promotion price comparisons like $19.08 vs $13.52, and 24% vs 29% average discount). Sample insight services include Market Content Review, SWOT deep dives across 3 retailers / 3 categories / 3 brands, competitor benchmarking, NPD reviews, tentpole event analysis (e.g., Prime Day), and customizable credit-based deliverables.

The deck clearly explains the commercial model: ExpertIQ Insights & Advisory is an annual subscription starting at $25K with volume discounts and flexible credit allocation across the year. It references internal-only assets (Menu & Rate Card, FAQ) and external collateral (ExpertIQ Datasheet, anonymized case studies, AMC and DSO report examples). It also differentiates ExpertIQ from AllyAI Media Teammate 1-click reports (generative AI summaries and executive-ready PPT/Excel exports) by highlighting the deeper advisory, custom SKU universe scoping, campaign-level tailoring, and strategic recommendations available through ExpertIQ.

Use this document when someone asks: “What is ExpertIQ?”, “How do we sell ExpertIQ?”, “What’s included in the $25K subscription?”, “How do AMC reports differ from in-platform dashboards?”, “What’s the credit model?”, “How do we position ExpertIQ vs AllyAI?”, or “What collateral can AEs use?” It is particularly useful for internal onboarding of new AEs or preparing for second-call discussions focused on upselling advisory services.

Not to confuse with the ExpertIQ Datasheet (external, customer-facing summary), the External Menu (client-ready list of services), or specific AMC/DSO report examples (tactical deliverables). This training deck is internal-only and combines positioning, pricing, analytics methodology, and sales process guidance in one consolidated enablement resource.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Flywheel Comparison - a competitive battle card designed to arm sales teams with clear differentiation between CommerceIQ and Flywheel in retail media and omni-commerce optimization. A battle card is a sales enablement document used in live selling situations to position against a specific competitor, highlight strengths and weaknesses, and provide talk tracks and probing questions. This document is used when a prospect is evaluating Flywheel or already working with them and CommerceIQ needs to differentiate on technology, incrementality, and enterprise-grade retail intelligence.

The document contrasts capabilities across several structured sections: Budget Optimization (CommerceIQ offers automated hourly bid and budget optimization with mid-month budget pacing adjustments vs Flywheel’s manual budget pacing and no hourly bidder), Incrementality (CommerceIQ’s ML-based incrementality ROAS (iROAS) model using Share of Voice and ROAS inputs to measure true total POS lift vs Flywheel’s traditional ad-attributed ROAS only), and Target Market (CommerceIQ focused on large enterprise brands vs Flywheel’s strength with small 3P sellers). It also outlines Retail Coverage (CommerceIQ supporting Amazon, Walmart, Instacart, Kroger, Target, Albertsons, Best Buy, Lowe’s, Costco and 100+ retailers vs Flywheel limited to Amazon and Walmart).

A major focus is Retail-Aware Advertising: CommerceIQ integrates on-hand and open PO inventory data, item-level competitive mapping, elasticity modeling, and profit-aware advertising, while noting Flywheel lacks Vendor Central integration, automated inventory-aware advertising, and dynamic competitive mapping. The document further highlights Share of Voice Optimization (tracking several thousand keywords driving >80% of category sales, weighted and item-level SOV, full SOV integration into automation) versus Flywheel not tracking SOV or search rankings in bid optimization. Share Growth Capability includes automated competitive out-of-stock (OOS) conquesting and full market SOV insights across retailers, contrasted with Flywheel’s manual identification and no automated competitor monitoring. DSP and Amazon Marketing Cloud integration is emphasized: CommerceIQ integrates DSP and AMC, supports multi-touch attribution tables and Search + Display + OTT measurement, while Flywheel lacks AMC integration and DSP product support.

The deck also includes specific sales talk tracks and challenger questions for champions, such as: "How do we know we're optimizing for true incremental sales (total POS vs ad-attributed)?", "Is your media mix factoring in profitability, market share, and chargebacks?", and "Does performance vary by account manager?" It reinforces CommerceIQ’s positioning as a unified omni-commerce platform with a single source of truth bridging retail and media, emphasizing technology-driven consistency versus service-led variability.

Use this document when a prospect asks: "How are you different from Flywheel?", "Do you support incrementality modeling?", "Does Flywheel integrate AMC or DSP?", "Can you optimize based on inventory and profitability?", or "Who has broader retailer coverage beyond Amazon?" It is especially useful in late-stage deals where Flywheel is shortlisted or incumbent.

Not to confuse with: a generic CommerceIQ product overview deck (which covers overall capabilities without competitor framing), a first-call deck (which introduces the platform at a high level), or a pricing document (which outlines commercial models). This document is specifically competitor-focused and structured for differentiation.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Ascential/Omnicom Competitive Battle Card (Updated May 2024) – a sales enablement battle card designed to help CommerceIQ reps compete against Ascential/Omnicom solutions (including Flywheel and Edge by Ascential). A battle card is a competitive-facing document used in live sales situations to arm account executives with positioning, differentiation points, FUD (Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt) questions, rebuttals, and feature comparisons. This document is specifically used when facing Omnicom-owned Flywheel, Edge’s LBA (Location-Based Analytics), or related Digital Shelf and Retail Media offerings.

The document covers detailed breakdowns of Edge’s LBA product, including the Overview tab (aggregated availability, distribution, and promotions across locations), Product tab (SKU-level views by retailer with filters for availability, in promotion, not in promotion, and average price), and Locations tab (sortable, searchable, filterable store-level data with chart views of availability over time). It highlights that LBA is based on store-level (not zipcode) data across 2,000 retailers where click-and-collect data exists, and notes limitations such as inability to decipher share of sales (using Share of Search as a proxy instead). It also calls out that certain scorecard metrics (Traffic, Conversion, Pricing, Availability) are owned-item only, with competitive data limited to Promotions and some Ratings & Reviews.

On the CommerceIQ side, the battle card emphasizes CommerceIQ Flywheel capabilities such as hourly bid adjustments, full-day campaign coverage (dayparting), budget pacing including mid-month budget changes, day-of-week optimization, and over-indexing during events like Prime Day. It contrasts this with competitors’ manual budget pacing and lack of hourly bidders. It highlights AI-Driven Demand Forecasting, granular data-driven optimization, real-time insights, automated campaign optimization, and a data transparency dashboard. It also outlines onboarding timelines (8–12 weeks for core onboarding; 2–4 weeks for Market Share when using Amazon catalog) and machine crawling that gathers product attributes without relying on Amazon’s categorization.

The Market Share (MS) section details MarketView (sales and share analysis vs competitors at categorical and subcategory levels), customizable reporting (with additional cost for customized taxonomy beyond Amazon’s default), a 6-section Scorecard explaining sales/share changes, and a cost-effective entry model offering the first 5–10 Amazon categories free as part of a bundled offer. It positions CommerceIQ on data accuracy, reliability, comprehensive competitive insights (pricing, content optimization, advertising tactics), and integrated ecosystem advantages. The document also emphasizes global scale (900+ retailers in 50+ countries), dedicated customer success, regional language support, and integrated platform flexibility.

Use this document if someone asks: “How does CommerceIQ compare to Flywheel?”, “What are Edge LBA limitations?”, “How do we position against Omnicom?”, “Does Flywheel support hourly bidding?”, “How do we compete on Market Share analytics?”, or “What FUD questions should I ask against Ascential?” It is specifically designed for competitive deal strategy and objection handling in mid-to-late stage sales cycles.

This document is explicitly competitive and tactical.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Skai Competitive Battle Card (Updated Sept 2024) - a detailed internal battle-card used by CommerceIQ sales teams to position against Skai in competitive Retail Media Management (RMM) deals. A battle-card is a tactical sales enablement document designed to help reps quickly understand a competitor’s strengths, weaknesses, pricing model, positioning, and common objections, along with recommended FUD (fear, uncertainty, doubt) questions and differentiation talking points. This document is used in live deals where Skai is present or likely to be shortlisted.

The document begins with a company overview of Skai: founded in 2006, led by CEO Yoav Izhar-Prato, part of Kenshoo, with investors including Bain Capital Ventures and Sequoia Capital Israel, and operations in 13 countries. It lists known clients such as L’Oréal, Bose, Reckitt, and Central Pet, as well as former clients (Emerson and McCaughey). It outlines Skai’s core positioning as an RMM platform with strengths in Google Ads management, cross-channel bulk editing, and integration with non-retail media. It also details why Skai wins (cheaper pricing at 1–2% of ad spend, margins driven by Google Ads, strong search advertising capabilities) and why they lose (UI/UX challenges, cumbersome workflow changes, inflexible reporting, Amazon campaign delays).

A large portion of the battle card contrasts Skai with CommerceIQ across key capability pillars: Dayparting (CIQ’s hourly adjustments and intra-day budget release vs Skai’s less nuanced approach), Share Growth (CIQ’s automatic competitive OOS conquesting and full SOV automation vs Skai’s limited capabilities requiring Profitero integration), Share of Voice Optimization (CIQ tracks 4,000 keywords daily, weighted SOV, standard shelves out of the box vs Skai tracking ~50 keywords and no item-level SOV), Budget Optimization (CIQ’s automated pacing and event-based over-indexing vs Skai’s insights not linked to automated actions), and Incrementality (CIQ’s AI-based iROAS incorporating SOV, search rankings, shopper propensity vs Skai’s recently launched, non-automated incrementality metric). It also highlights API automation differences and global retailer coverage (120+ retailers via API for CIQ vs ~100 for Skai).

The document includes specific pricing intelligence: Skai typically charges 1–2% of ad spend (often closer to 1% for agencies), has offered flat-rate “all you can eat” pricing driving effective rates below 0.5%, and is introducing self-serve models below 1%. It claims Skai subsidizes retail media pricing with Google Ads revenue. It also references Skai Labs (custom development services announced May 2024) and Skai’s April 2024 incrementality announcement. The deck embeds structured FUD questions sales reps can use, such as probing Skai’s retail-aware data integration (inventory, profitability, elasticity), whitespace keyword identification, incrementality credibility, flexibility of reporting, and level of automation.

Use this document when a prospect says they are evaluating Skai, when pricing pressure arises due to Skai’s lower fee structure, when asked about Skai’s incrementality claims, or when differentiating on Share of Voice, retail-aware media, or AI-driven automation. It is especially useful in mid-to-late stage competitive deals requiring tactical positioning.

Not to confuse with: the RMM Second Call Deck (which is a full product presentation of CommerceIQ capabilities), the Product Box (which defines CommerceIQ’s positioning and packaging), or customer case study decks (which focus on proof points rather than competitive comparison). This document is strictly competitive intelligence and objection-handling focused.

Version: Updated September 2024. The document includes references to April 2024 and May 2024 competitive updates (Skai incrementality launch and Skai Labs announcement), indicating it is an actively maintained competitive asset.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Pacvue Competitive Battle Card - ESM (Updated Sept 25) - a competitive sales battle card designed to help CommerceIQ sellers position against Pacvue in both ESM (Discover & Guide) and Retail Media Management (Activate) deals. A battle card is a concise but detailed competitive enablement document used during live sales cycles to handle objections, differentiate capabilities, and guide discovery conversations. This document is specifically for competitive situations where Pacvue is present or incumbent.

The document provides side-by-side comparisons across key pillars: Content Audit & Optimization, Share of Voice (SOV) Optimization, Budget Optimization, Customization, Reporting, Forecasting, Inventory-Aware Advertising, and Market Share Insights. For content, CommerceIQ emphasizes automated content completeness measurement, direct PIM/DAM integration, daily auto-ticketing of noncompliant changes, and AI-driven taxonomy—contrasted with Pacvue’s manual audits and reliance on partners like Profitero and Vizit. For SOV, CommerceIQ highlights tracking several thousand keywords representing 80%+ of category sales, weighted and item-level SOV, and full SOV integration into campaign automation. Pacvue is positioned as limited to several hundred keywords, % visibility tracking, and SOV not feeding into automation logic.

In Retail Media (Activate), the battle card contrasts CommerceIQ’s IROAS-based optimization, multiplier-adjusted CPC, last bid change lookback, inventory and profit-aware advertising, and simplified budget pacing playbooks against Pacvue’s sandbox-style customization, pivot-table-like reporting, and forecasting across advertising, marketing, sales, and supply chain (with noted unverifiable accuracy). It calls out Pacvue’s partial retail data integration, lack of automated inventory-aware bidding (only on-hand inventory tracking), reliance on external integrations (e.g., Profitero), and fragmented point-solution positioning. CommerceIQ is framed as an all-in-one AI platform operating across 90+ retailers (Amazon, Amazon DSP, Walmart, Criteo, Citrus, Instacart, Kroger/PromoteIQ, Albertsons, and more), with unified digital shelf, market share, and DSP capabilities.

The document includes structured FUD discovery questions for reps to use in live conversations, such as: whether content audits are automated or manual, whether OOS prediction and Vendor Initiated Orders (VIOs) are supported, whether media investments are incremental vs organic, and how quickly teams respond to competitor pricing and share shifts. It also includes competitive pitch positioning language framing Pacvue as a fragmented point solution with agency dependencies and manual workflows, versus CommerceIQ’s unified AI-driven automation with real-time insights and autonomous actions (including profit recovery ticket automation and OOS prediction).

Use this document when a prospect says they use Pacvue, are evaluating Pacvue vs CommerceIQ, or ask about differences in SOV tracking, automation sophistication, inventory-aware bidding, content compliance automation, or reporting customization. Opportunities include deeper supply chain integrations (inventory on hand, PO data, dropship) and DSM integrations (e.g., scraped coupons for ad optimization). For Skai, strengths center on cross-channel data integrations (including paid social), while weaknesses emphasize limited native activation and reliance on partners. Strategic recommendations are embedded (e.g., "Don’t go feature-by-feature. Win on full platform value" and "Partner with them on RMM tech").

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Dimetyd Battle Card (Updated Dec 23) - a competitive battle card designed to help CommerceIQ sales reps compete effectively against Dimetyd in Profit Recovery Automation (PRA) deals. A battle card is a sales enablement document that provides side-by-side comparisons, objection handling, FUD questions, pricing contrasts, win/loss analysis, and positioning guidance for live sales conversations. This document is specifically used when Dimetyd is present in a deal or when a prospect references FinOps-style recovery vendors.

The document covers a detailed feature comparison between CommerceIQ and Dimetyd across core recovery categories: Chargebacks (Rejected PO Rate, PO On Time, ASIN accuracy), Quantity Shortages (30-60-90 day automated disputes vs once-a-year/quarter historical lookbacks up to 36 months), Co-Op Disputes (invalid deduction identification and automated filing), and Price Variance (SKU-level analysis of Item Cost per AVC, PO Cost, Invoice Cost, Amazon Paid Cost). Pricing comparisons are explicit: Dimetyd typically charges 30% of recovery or offers a fixed monthly fee (with notes that deals have been lost on the fixed option), while CommerceIQ positions competitive, transparent pricing with broader recovery coverage. documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the CommerceIQ-Quarterly-Industry-Trends-2025-Q1-report-April-2025-va - a quarterly industry trends enablement report summarizing ecommerce performance in Q1 2025 using aggregated data from CommerceIQ’s REM Platform for Amazon sellers (October 2023–March 2025). An enablement guide of this type is designed to arm sales, customer success, and marketing teams with data-backed insights and category benchmarks to drive strategic conversations with brands and retailers.

The report begins with a total industry overview titled “The State of Ecommerce: Q1 2025.” Key macro findings include declining ROAS year-over-year despite increased ad spend, potentially driven by rising CPCs; a 2.5% YoY increase in dollars lost due to out-of-stocks (OOS) in Q1; and RepOOS% trending down from a 4.1% Prime Day peak toward Amazon’s 2% benchmark. Across many categories, overall sales slowed relative to Q1 2024, with unit margins declining approximately 7%, signaling broad profitability pressure.

The document then provides category-level deep dives. Examples include: Office Products revenue lost due to OOS declining 25% YoY, with stable glance views and 6% YoY sales growth; Patio, Lawn & Garden inventory rising 16% YoY; Electronics showing a 12-month downward trend in RepOOS% despite seasonal OOS spikes; Health & Personal Care seeing 10% YoY ad spend growth but a 30% ROAS decline (March vs. March), alongside a 6% YoY increase in OOS revenue loss and an 18-month upward RepOOS% trend; Home & Kitchen experiencing a 25% YoY ad spend increase with 2.5% ROAS improvement in March but a 43% YoY surge in OOS revenue losses; and Tools & Home achieving 1.6% YoY sales growth, margins near 18-month highs, and a 32% decline in OOS-related revenue loss.

Additional category insights include: Beauty with 40% YoY order volume growth and 14% traffic growth; Pet Products inventory up 31% YoY reaching an 18-month high; Grocery ASP declining 5% YoY with increased discounting; Toys seeing 11% YoY ad spend decline but stronger ROAS during peak periods; and Furniture experiencing a 192% YoY spike in March OOS revenue loss. The report repeatedly analyzes key metrics such as AD SPEND | ROAS | CPC, GLANCE VIEWS (traffic), OPS vs. Unit Margin %, PRICE LEVEL vs. DISCOUNT %, ON HAND INVENTORY, and REVENUE LOSS DUE TO OOS.

documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the “Henkel: Winning the Next Wave of Search – How Generative AI is Reshaping Retail” enablement guide – a strategic sales presentation tailored to Henkel that explains how generative AI is disrupting retail search and what CommerceIQ enables in response. An enablement guide is a customer-facing strategic narrative used by sales teams to educate enterprise brands on a market shift (in this case, GEO – Generative Engine Optimization) and position CommerceIQ’s platform as the solution. It is best used in executive-level or strategy discussions where the customer needs transformation guidance rather than just product features.

The document begins by contrasting the traditional SEO-driven shopper journey (Need > Awareness > Search query > Browse results > Compare options > Purchase) with the new agentic AI path (Need > Ask > Answer > Purchase). It uses Persil Non Bio laundry detergent as a stage-by-stage example across Awareness, Consideration, Purchase, and Post-Purchase. It explains how LLMs now narrow options automatically, reduce visible SKUs to only a handful of recommendations, and increasingly support direct checkout experiences such as “Shop with Rufus.” It emphasizes that content quality, structured data, trust signals (ratings and sentiment), and hyper-relevance now determine visibility. It also cites Adobe data showing generative AI-powered shopping rising 4,700% without traffic to traditional retail sites.

A core section explains the divergence between open and closed AI ecosystems. Amazon (Rufus) is described as a proprietary, vertically integrated LLM prioritizing detailed PDPs, deep catalog attributes, conversational Q&A, and image/video SEO. Open ecosystems (e.g., Shopify merchants leveraging OpenAI and external data sources) prioritize consistent brand narrative, broad content syndication, and strong metadata/schema implementation. The document stresses that Henkel must compete in both environments. It introduces CommerceIQ Digital Shelf Optimization (DSO) as the foundation for GEO readiness, validating attributes, titles, images, PIM integrations, schema markup, and SKU completeness. It also details how review sentiment monitoring, Q&A mining, and competitive benchmarking turn ratings and reviews into a growth engine for AI discoverability.

The guide then outlines 9 GEO-focused principles, including: being AI-visible through structured, machine-readable PDPs; going beyond keyword-optimized titles; writing conversational, shopper-intent-driven copy; leveraging social proof; redefining visibility as paid and organic converge; creating smarter ads that highlight meaningful differentiators; and unifying paid and organic performance. It explains how Retail Media Management (RMM) and Digital Shelf Optimization (DSO) connect performance signals across retail media and AI-driven discovery. AllyAI Media Teammate is positioned as an agentic optimization engine making thousands of bid and budget decisions daily, analyzing 50+ signals across digital shelf, traffic, inventory, competition, and retail channels to optimize incrementality, share of voice, and iROAS in real time. AI Outcomes Manager is referenced as the measurement layer driving continuous improvement.

Use this document when someone asks: “How is generative AI changing retail search?”, “What is GEO and how should Henkel prepare?”, “How does CommerceIQ help brands win in Amazon Rufus or AI shopping environments?”, “How do paid media and organic AI search converge?”, or “How do reviews influence LLM product recommendations?” It is ideal for strategic transformation conversations, especially with digital commerce, ecommerce, or retail media leaders.

A battle card is a concise, field-facing competitive document that outlines how to position against a specific competitor, why CIQ wins or loses, pricing dynamics, differentiators, and suggested talk tracks. This document is intended for live sales conversations, RFP responses, and competitive deal strategy.

The document includes a company overview of SupplyPike: founded in 2018, acquired by SPS Commerce for $206M in August 2024, previously led by CEO Dan Sanker, with $25M Series B raised in 2022 from Noro-Moseley Partners, Frontier Growth, and Blumberg Capital. The core of the battle card contrasts SupplyPike’s “reactive” and retailer-specific approach with CommerceIQ’s AI-powered, unified commerce platform. It provides suggested response talk tracks, competitive pitch positioning language, and FUD-style discovery questions such as: “Can your deductions system connect insights to your retail media spend and inventory planning to prevent future losses?” and “When recovery rates plateau, what advanced capabilities help you identify new recovery opportunities?”

Use this document when a prospect mentions SupplyPike, when responding to an RFP where SupplyPike is shortlisted, when handling pricing objections tied to flat-fee PRA vendors, or when preparing for a competitive pitch focused on Amazon deduction recovery. documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the AI Goal Optimizer - External Customer Deck, a detailed second-call sales presentation designed to educate prospects and customers on CommerceIQ’s AI Goal Optimizer (AGO) and AllyAI Media Teammate. A second-call deck is used after initial discovery to go deep into product functionality, differentiators, setup process, performance impact, and proof points. This deck positions AI Goal Optimizer as an AI-powered system that integrates bidding, budgeting, and incrementality-based campaign optimization into one unified workflow for retail media management.

The deck begins by outlining key industry challenges: lack of real-time incrementality solutions, inefficient media management tools, and sales cannibalization caused by traditional ROAS-only measurement. It contrasts human-only optimization (<10 optimizations/day), human + rules-based automation (<100/day), and human + AI (4000+ optimizations/day). It introduces CommerceIQ’s proprietary algorithm that dynamically allocates campaign budgets and keyword bids daily, with hourly bid adjustments using 50+ signals across digital shelf, media, inventory, traffic, spend, SOV (Share of Voice), ROAS, and iROAS. The system identifies efficient spend allocation across campaigns and keywords, increasing budgets for high iROAS segments and decreasing budgets for low iROAS segments while staying within predefined constraints.

A core section focuses on incrementality modeling. The deck explains how traditional siloed ROAS optimization leads to misaligned priorities due to lack of digital shelf connectivity. CommerceIQ’s Incrementality Modeling incorporates forward-looking digital shelf signals and organic Share of Voice (SOV) dynamics. It outlines a three-phase maturity curve: Phase 1 establishes an incrementality factor based on starting digital shelf position; Phase 2 shows organic SOV growth as advertising increases sales velocity; Phase 3 shows organic SOV saturation, declining iROAS, and automatic budget reduction. The model continuously evolves to account for ad-driven organic ranking improvement, enabling automated optimization based on iROAS rather than ROAS alone.

The deck includes detailed product workflow content via an “easy five-step process”: (1) Define budget timeframe, levels (category, brand, user-defined segments), and optimization metrics (ROAS, iROAS, SoV); (2) Enter monthly budgets and goal values; (3) Specify events and seasonality; (4) Enter spend constraints by keyword, targeting, and campaign types; and (5) Choose optimization approach—Rules-Based Automation or Goal Optimization for iROAS with AllyAI Media Teammate II. It highlights dashboard visibility, planned vs. actual budget pacing, and customizable budget allocations (e.g., allocating 30% of budget to 5 days for tentpole events). The product is currently available for Amazon and Walmart, with additional retailers coming soon.

Performance proof points include a Pilgrim’s Pride case study featuring Aaron Conkey (Sr. Associate Digital Marketing Manager) citing significant iROAS and sales improvements with CPC reductions. Quantified results shown include +75% growth in ad sales, -12.8% CPC reduction, and +55% improvement in incremental sales efficiency across 10 brands on Amazon and Walmart. The deck also references finalist recognition in the Walmart Connect Partner Network Awards and showcases AllyAI optimizing thousands of keywords using 50+ signals.

Use this deck when a prospect asks for a deep dive into AI Goal Optimizer functionality, incrementality modeling methodology, how CommerceIQ optimizes iROAS in real time, how AllyAI works across thousands of keywords, or for proof points and case studies on Amazon and Walmart. It is especially relevant for retail media leaders evaluating AI-driven budget reallocation, digital shelf-connected optimization, and automated bid management.

It explains why ROAS alone cannot predict true incremental growth and introduces the Incrementality Factor (IF) as a core metric. A major section details AllyAI’s automation phases: Phase 1 begins with highly incremental keywords; Phase 2 drives incremental sales and increases Organic Share of Voice (SOV); Phase 3 reduces iROAS as organic rank improves and cannibalization decreases; Phase 4 automatically shifts bids toward higher iROAS keywords. The deck emphasizes that AllyAI performs 4,000+ optimizations per day compared to <10 manual or <100 rules-based optimizations. documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Teikametrics Comparison - a competitive battle card that outlines the detailed feature-by-feature differences between CommerceIQ and Teikametrics across advertising automation, retail data integration, share of voice tracking, Amazon Marketing Cloud (AMC), incrementality measurement, and omnichannel support. A battle card is a sales enablement document designed to help sales teams position against a specific competitor in live calls, RFP responses, and objection handling scenarios. This document is intended for competitive selling situations where Teikametrics is being evaluated alongside CommerceIQ.

The document is structured as a side-by-side comparison under the theme “Winning Omnichannel with CommerceIQ,” and breaks down capabilities by functional category. In Share Growth Capability, CommerceIQ highlights automatic flagging of competitive out-of-stock (OOS) conquesting opportunities, full market Share of Voice (SOV) and traffic insights across all retailers, and AI-based automation for generic, branded, and conquesting keyword classification. In contrast, Teikametrics relies on manual classification of generic/branded/competitive keywords. In the Amazon Marketing Cloud section, CommerceIQ offers fully integrated AMC capabilities within the platform, including performance reporting across Search + Display and Search + Display + OTT, as well as a multi-touch attribution table. Teikametrics does not have in-platform AMC capabilities and instead offers custom reporting when working directly with their team.

The document also compares supported platforms and retail-aware advertising depth. CommerceIQ supports AMS, DSP, Walmart, Criteo, Citrus, Instacart, and Kroger (noted as Q3), and claims the ability to onboard new retailers in 2–3 weeks. Teikametrics supports AMS and Walmart, and may manage DSP but without native in-platform buildout. In Retail-Aware Advertising, CommerceIQ integrates retail data fully into ad optimization, incorporates on-hand and open PO inventory data, includes item-level competitive mapping and elasticity modeling, and enables inventory and profit-aware advertising. Teikametrics only partially integrates retail data into ad adjustments and tracks on-hand inventory without automated inventory-aware advertising.

Further differentiation appears in Share of Voice Optimization and Budget Optimization. CommerceIQ tracks several thousand keywords that drive more than 80% of sales, offers weighted SOV and item-level SOV, and fully integrates SOV into automation. Teikametrics tracks a limited number of keywords (75–200), focuses on Brand Coverage in Search (BCS) rather than weighted SOV, and offers Organic, Paid, and Total BCS with only partial integration into ad optimization. For Budget Optimization, CommerceIQ provides budget pacing with mid-month optimization adjustments, automated day-of-week budget optimization, and the ability to over-index spend during events like Prime Day. Teikametrics supports monthly budget pacing and optimization based on conversion rate, seasonality, inventory levels, and price changes. In Incrementality, CommerceIQ promotes a first-of-its-kind incrementality ROAS (iROAS), built via machine learning to combine SOV and ROAS for true ad impact measurement, while Teikametrics relies solely on traditional ROAS-based optimization.

Use this document when a prospect says “We’re considering Teikametrics,” “How are you different from Teikametrics?”, “Do you support AMC natively?”, “How do you handle SOV vs BCS?”, or “Do you offer incrementality measurement beyond ROAS?” It is especially useful in competitive deal cycles, renewal defense conversations, and RFP comparisons where automation depth, retail integration, and measurement sophistication are key decision factors.

This is the ExpertIQ Expert Insights FAQ – Internal - a structured internal enablement FAQ that outlines how the ExpertIQ credit-based subscription model works, including pricing, packaging, ARR treatment, contract terms, expiration rules, reporting options, and operational workflows. An enablement guide like this is used by sales, account managers, and customer-facing teams to answer detailed commercial and operational questions about a product. The document details the ExpertIQ credit packages, including the core annual subscription starting at $25,000 for 120 credits (10 per month equivalent), with scaled discounts: $70,000 for 360 annual credits (3-package bundle with $5K discount) and $150,000 for 840 annual credits (7-package bundle with $25K discount). Additional ad-hoc credits are available in bundles of 10 for $2,100. It clarifies that subscription packages starting at $25K count toward ARR goals, while the $2,100 10-credit ad-hoc bundles do not count toward ARR. It also notes that pricing may increase over time, though the number of credits included will remain the same.

The FAQ covers contract terms and credit expiration policies in detail. Annual subscription credits are valid for one year and are planned across quarterly deliverables with flexibility based on business needs. Up to 10 credits may be carried over into the next contract term if the customer remains subscribed to CommerceIQ base products (RMM, ACP, DSO). Ad-hoc 10-credit packages expire within 90 days of signed PO or at contract end—whichever comes first—with a specific example showing a September 1 purchase and September 30 contract end resulting in expiration on September 30 (earlier of 90 days or contract end).

Operationally, the document explains that customers work with a CommerceIQ Insights Manager to plan deliverables on an optimal quarterly cadence, though shorter or longer timelines can be accommodated depending on scope and resources. It outlines report options such as DSO Insights and Amazon Marketing Cloud (AMC, formerly AMC+) reports, with credit cost varying per report. Menu updates are communicated quarterly, and support questions are directed to expertiq@commerceiq.ai. It also references internal resources such as the ExpertIQ SKU List and Rate Card (Internal Only) and an External Menu used for customer communication.

Use this document if someone asks: "Does ExpertIQ count toward ARR?", "How do ExpertIQ credits expire?", "What happens if a client has a global footprint?", "Can credits be used across markets?", "What is included in the $25K package?", "How do quarterly planning sessions work?", or "What happens if the contract is less than one year?" documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the ICP 1,2,3 Definitions - an internal enablement guide that formally defines CommerceIQ’s Ideal Customer Profile tiers based on company revenue and product category focus. An ICP definition document establishes which types of companies sales and marketing should prioritize, how accounts are segmented (e.g., enterprise vs mid-market), and what qualification thresholds apply. This document is used to align sales targeting, territory planning, pipeline qualification, and strategic focus.

The document defines three primary ICP tiers. ICP 1: Enterprise CPG includes CPG brands with greater than or equal to $1 billion USD in total annual revenue. Categories covered under ICP 1 include Health & Household, Grocery & Gourmet Food, Pet Supplies, Beauty & Personal Care, Baby Products, Alcohol, and Toys & Games. ICP 2: Mid-Market CPG includes CPG brands with annual revenue greater than or equal to $300 million USD and less than $1 billion USD, covering the same CPG-focused categories (Health & Household, Grocery & Gourmet Food, Pet Supplies, Beauty & Personal Care, Baby Products, Toys & Games, Alcohol).

ICP 3: Enterprise Hardlines defines non-CPG Hardlines brands with greater than or equal to $1 billion USD in total annual revenue. Hardlines categories explicitly listed include Home & Kitchen, Tools & Home Improvement, Patio, Lawn & Garden, Furniture/Decor, Kitchen & Dining, Sports & Outdoors, Automotive, and Electronics. The segmentation clearly distinguishes between CPG and Hardlines verticals while using revenue as the primary qualification metric, with $1B as the enterprise threshold and $300M–$1B as the mid-market band for CPG.

If someone asks, “What qualifies as ICP 1 vs ICP 2?”, “What revenue threshold defines enterprise?”, “Do Hardlines brands fall into ICP 1 or ICP 3?”, or “Is a $500M Beauty brand in scope?”, this is the document to use. It is also the reference point for territory design, account prioritization, TAM analysis, and sales compensation alignment tied to ICP coverage.

Not to confuse with: a Target Account List (which would list specific company names), a Product Box (which defines product positioning and features), or a Pricing Guide (which outlines commercial terms). This document does not include customer names, pricing, product capabilities, or case studies—only ICP segmentation criteria.

documents.documentIdentity: This is the Content Agent Messaging Framework – a structured messaging guide that defines how to position AllyAI’s Content Agent for the Commercial / Sales Buyer, including core value propositions, buyer-specific pain points, differentiation, proof points, objection handling, and talk tracks tailored to revenue-driving sales teams.
documents.comprehensiveDescription:
This is the Content Agent Messaging Framework – a talk-track and positioning guide that outlines how to message AllyAI’s Content Agent to Commercial and Sales buyers. A Messaging Framework is a sales enablement document that standardizes how a product is described, differentiated, and justified to a specific persona. Unlike a product deck (which visually presents features) or a product box (which defines the product commercially), this document provides structured language, value pillars, and persona-specific narratives sales teams use in live calls, emails, and presentations.

The document centers on positioning the AllyAI Content Agent specifically for Commercial / Sales stakeholders, reframing content optimization as a revenue-driving lever rather than a marketing task. It outlines core buyer pain points such as missed sales due to poor PDP content, inconsistent retailer execution, slow content updates, lack of visibility into content performance, and manual workflows between sales and eCommerce teams. It then maps these pains to value pillars including revenue growth, improved digital shelf conversion, faster retailer compliance, and scalable content optimization across accounts.

Inside, the framework details key messaging components: primary value proposition statements, supporting proof points, feature-to-benefit translations, differentiation versus manual processes and internal content teams, objection handling guidance, and persona-specific impact statements tied to sales KPIs. It includes positioning guidance on how to articulate Content Agent as an AI-powered assistant that proactively identifies content gaps, recommends optimizations, and enables sales teams to drive retailer performance without relying solely on marketing resources. The structure likely includes sections such as: Buyer Overview, Core Messaging Pillars, Key Differentiators, Proof Points, Objection Handling, and Suggested Discovery Questions.

The framework also guides how to anchor conversations around measurable commercial outcomes—such as improved conversion, increased digital shelf visibility, faster time to content correction, and revenue lift—while emphasizing alignment with retailer requirements and joint business planning goals. It provides language that shifts the narrative from ‘content management’ to ‘sales acceleration through digital shelf optimization.’

Use this document when someone asks: “How should we position Content Agent to a VP of Sales?”, “What’s the commercial value of Content Agent?”, “What’s the talk track for Content Agent in a sales call?”, “How do we explain Content Agent to a revenue leader?”, or “What messaging should we use for Commercial buyers?”

Not to confuse with: a Content Agent Product Box (which would define pricing, packaging, and commercial structure), a First Call Deck (high-level introductory presentation), a Second Call Deck (deep feature walkthrough), or a Battle Card (competitive comparison vs a specific competitor). This document is specifically a persona-based messaging and positioning framework for Commercial/Sales audiences.
